sources.title: Here’s how scientists aim to speed up drug development for treating new viruses

items.title: One Cheap Starting Material, Dozens of Antiviral Candidates
items.body: Writing in The Conversation Canada, researchers describe a modular approach that turns one cheap starting material into a wide range of finished drug candidates within weeks. Using it, they say they made dozens of new molecules and, in early laboratory tests, identified three with promising anti-HIV activity. Their stated motivation: there is a surprisingly limited arsenal of drugs that reliably fight viral infections, which is why faster routes to new candidates carry weight beyond the individual molecules they produce. Modularity is the interesting part. The logic is throughput over polish — build breadth first, then let testing decide which candidates deserve the slow, expensive attention. Activity in early laboratory tests is a first look rather than a verdict, and that is exactly why a route cheap enough to feed many compounds into that first look is worth having.

sources.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5022-5028: Cashing in at Cache Creek

discussion.body: The rectangles are the real invention here. Long before a rock matters scientifically, it matters logistically — an unnamed target is just an argument about which rock you mean.

There is an odd symmetry in naming Martian parcels after small towns whose significance is geological. Mars gets explored with a gazetteer borrowed from Earth's rock towns, which is charming and a little circular.

items.title: Before Curiosity Landed, Gale Crater Was Cut Into Rectangles With Earthly Names
items.body: Long before the rover arrived, the area of Gale crater that Curiosity would explore was divided into rectangular parcels, each with a designated name. Those names were drawn from small towns associated with significant geological features, so a patch of Mars carries the label of a place on Earth that earned its fame from rock. Inside each rectangle, targets picked out by the mission — mesas, bedrock, soil, boulders — were then given unofficial names based on the theme of that parcel. That is how a foreign landscape becomes workable. A team spending months inside one quad needs to be able to say “drill there” and have everyone picture the same object, and a shared theme makes the vocabulary stick. The naming is administrative and unromantic, and it may be the reason the science can be argued about at all: you cannot debate a contact between rock layers that nobody can name.

sources.title: Mapping the Gaps in NASA’s Return to the Moon, featuring Richard Spolzino

discussion.body: Notice what the deliverable is: not a component, but a list of unknowns. That is the kind of work that gets trimmed first and regretted longest.
A catalogue of gaps is still bounded by what the team already suspects might be missing. Where does the part nobody thought to ask about get handled?

items.title: An Engineer Whose Job Is to Find What NASA Doesn't Yet Know
items.body: Richard Spolzino, an aerospace engineer, works at NASA's Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, within Moon Base's mission architecture and systems interoperability effort. His task is to help identify what NASA still doesn't know about the Moon and Mars, and to make sure that missing information gets found before it becomes a problem. It is a job defined by questions rather than hardware. The framing Spolzino offers for his own choices is about reach: he says it kept coming back to where he could have the most impact, where his work could touch the most things. “Systems interoperability” sounds like a footnote until you consider what an unanswered question costs when it surfaces far from the drawing board — which is the whole argument for finding it early.

sources.title: 'This is home for me': Amber Marshall reflects as 20th season of Heartland set to begin

items.title: Twenty Seasons of Heartland, and Its Star Grew Up on the Show
items.body: CBC's Heartland is marking its 20th season. Amber Marshall has grown up on the long-running drama, which CBC describes as mirroring her real-life love of horses and ranch life, and the show's cast, characters and global fans keep finding comfort and connection in its stories. Comfort, on that reading, is the whole proposition: a series this old is selling return rather than surprise, which may be its own kind of accomplishment.

sources.title: Serb separatist Dodik declares victory in Bosnia vote as ethnic tensions and EU hopes collide

discussion.body: A presidency with three members, nationalist blocs set to occupy each of them, and 3.4 million voters choosing — that is an odd advertisement for the power-sharing idea.

The seat count is the least interesting part. DW calls Dodik a disqualified secessionist, and the candidate he backed still looks set to take a chair in the joint institution. That is the sentence to underline.

items.title: Bosnia's Three-Seat Presidency Is Set to Go Nationalist
items.body: Bosnia-Herzegovina's three-member presidency is set to be dominated by nationalists from the three major ethnic groups, Deutsche Welle reports — including Zeljka Cvijanovic, who was backed by Milorad Dodik, the Serb secessionist leader DW describes as disqualified. PBS NewsHour notes that around 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three presidency members and lawmakers for the national parliament. If that projection holds, a body built as a multi-ethnic institution ends up with all three of its chairs in nationalist hands, which is a result worth reading as a measure of party machinery as much as of public mood. The sharpest detail is Dodik's role: a man DW calls a disqualified secessionist is nonetheless positioned to have backed a winner in the joint presidency he would prefer to see weakened.

sources.title: ‘Spotlight’ Director Says The Catholic Church Hasn’t Done ‘Enough’ To Protect Children From Sexual Assault 10 Years After Film’s Best Picture Win: ‘Not Until Every Child Is Safe’

items.title: What 'Spotlight' Won Best Picture For: The Globe's Reporting on a Cover-Up
items.body: Tom McCarthy's Spotlight took Best Picture at the 2016 Academy Awards. Variety notes the ensemble — Michael Keaton, Rachel McAdams and Mark Ruffalo — and that the film's praise went to the way it chronicled the Boston Globe's investigative reporting, the work that exposed the Catholic Church's systemic cover-up of sexual abuse of children by priests. It is a drama built on journalism rather than a whodunit, and the antagonist is an institution rather than one monster, which is roughly the hardest thing to put on screen. A cover-up that is systemic has no convenient confession scene; praise for the chronicle, rather than for a twist, is praise for a film that trusted viewers to stay interested in how knowledge gets assembled.

sources.title: Antigonish, N.S., sign condemned for depicting rape culture

items.title: Antigonish Sign Draws Condemnation From Two Universities
items.body: A sign hung outside an off-campus house in Antigonish, N.S., during St. Francis Xavier University's homecoming weekend is being described as an example of rape culture, and CBC reports it drew condemnation from two universities and from a professor who teaches at St. FX. The uncomfortable part of stories like this is jurisdictional: off-campus houses sit in the gap between a university's rules and a town's authority, and homecoming is the weekend when that gap gets tested in public.

sources.title: Brazil election: Early count puts Bolsonaro ahead of Lula

items.title: Brazil's Early Count Puts Flávio Bolsonaro Ahead, While Polls Point to a Close Race
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that early results in Brazil's presidential election put Flávio Bolsonaro in front. Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, is running against the incumbent, Lula da Silva, who is described in the report as the left-wing candidate he took on in the race to lead Brazil's government. Sam Altman is not involved.

sources.title: AP report: U.S. Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack

items.title: The U.S. Air Force Has Brought Its Bombers Home From RAF Fairford
items.body: The U.S. Air Force has brought home the bombers it had stationed at a U.S.-run military air base in England, PBS NewsHour reports. The aircraft were based at RAF Fairford, which the report describes as a base used to strike Iran. The pullout follows an investigation into a planned terror attack at RAF Fairford. The result is a posture change: aircraft that formed part of the base's strike role are no longer sitting in England.

sources.title: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar

discussion.body: The name is doing a lot of work. A body called the Super Intelligence Force invites expectations of technical work — evaluations, model review, maybe procurement — while its stated mandate is coordinating government engagement with AI. Those are different jobs, and the label will be the yardstick whether or not it was meant to be.

Coordination is a real function, not a consolation prize. When several agencies and outside labs all want a single counterpart in the White House, being that counterpart is the whole product. A force that only convenes can still change what gets built and bought.

items.title: A 'Super Intelligence Force' Whose Stated Job Is Coordination
items.body: President Trump said Jay Clayton will lead the White House's new body, the Super Intelligence Force, which is to coordinate government engagement with artificial intelligence, NPR reports. Clayton is currently the national intelligence chief, per NPR's report on the appointment — an unusual résumé for a technology-facing role, and one that hints the White House is thinking about AI through a security and intelligence lens rather than a purely industrial one. The announcement names a leader and a mandate: coordination of how the government deals with AI. It does not, in what NPR reports, specify the force's authority, staff, or budget, so the practical question is whether it becomes a clearinghouse that agencies must route through or a convening shop that labs can take or leave. The title itself, with its leap past present-day systems to superintelligence, is worth noting: the rhetoric is about capability that does not yet exist, while the job described is the mundane work of getting a government to speak with one voice.

sources.title: Box Office: ‘Digger’ Majorly Bombs With $8 Million Opening Weekend, ‘Verity’ Scores $32 Million Debut

items.title: 'Digger' Opens to $8 Million From 3,321 Theaters
items.body: Variety reports that “Digger,” in which Tom Cruise plays a powerful oil tycoon bracing for an ecological disaster of epic proportions, opened to an $8 million weekend from 3,321 North American theaters — a result the trade calls an embarrassing collapse for a release on that many screens. Run the arithmetic and it comes to roughly $2,400 per theater, the sort of average that suggests the film's star and its wide footprint were doing very different amounts of work. Big-screen spectacle about a catastrophe, undone by one of its own.

sources.title: ‘The History Of Concrete’ Cracks $1 Million, ‘NAZA’ Lifts Off – Specialty Box Office

discussion.body: The appealing part is the subject matter doing the work: no true-crime hook, no celebrity, just a material everyone walks on, and it's the one leading the platform-release doc field.

The title is doing a lot of load-bearing here. Top platform-release documentary is not the same as top documentary, and specialty grosses are small enough that the comparison class changes the story entirely.

And the two films aren't even at the same stage: one is in week three with over $1.2 million built up, the other has five days and $86,000 behind it. Comparing the totals compares a marathon runner to someone just off the starting line.

items.title: A Documentary About Concrete Becomes the Year's Top-Grossing Platform-Release Doc
items.body: John Wilson's The History of Concrete, which premiered at Sundance and is being released by Magnolia Pictures, was eyeing $450,000 from 160 screens in its third week, Deadline reports, lifting its cumulative gross past $1.2 million and, by the trade's reckoning, making it the top-grossing platform-release documentary of 2026. In the same specialty roundup, Deadline reports that the acclaimed documentary NAZA took in a five-day gross of $86,000 since its theatrical debut on Wednesday. Two numbers, two very different moments: one film is three weeks into a slow platform build, the other is counting its first days. The crown here is also narrower than it sounds — top platform-release doc is a smaller title than the year's biggest documentary, and the figure that earns it is the sort of quiet milestone that only reads as a milestone inside the specialty market. Still, a film about concrete outgrossing the field has a certain satisfying logic to it.

sources.title: James Gunn Is Writing His Next Movie Following ‘Man of Tomorrow’: “Already In It”

discussion.body: A studio co-CEO who is still writing his own scripts is either reassuring or an admission that the bench behind him is thin, depending on your mood.
The quote only answers a question about whether he's ready to start writing. It isn't a slate announcement, and it shouldn't be read as one.
True, but the mechanics are still worth noting: a script in progress on one film while the edit is pending on another, both under the same writer's name.

items.title: James Gunn Says He's Already Writing the Film After 'Man of Tomorrow'
items.body: Deadline reports that James Gunn, co-CEO of DC Studios, is keeping his head down on his own work while Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. reshapes the studio landscape around him — a deal the trade describes as industry-shaking. Asked whether he was ready to begin writing the film that will follow Man of Tomorrow, Gunn said he is already in it, and Deadline notes he is still awaiting the edit on his upcoming sequel to 2025's Superman. It is a small, practical picture of how a studio executive's job overlaps with a writer's: pages going out on one project while an earlier film sits in the edit bay, with no release calendar attached. A quote about readiness is worth reading precisely for what it doesn't promise — it's momentum, not a schedule.

sources.title: Brazil votes, with Lula facing Bolsonaro's son

items.title: Brazil's Runoff Hangs on a 50% Threshold as Lula Faces Flávio Bolsonaro
items.body: Brazil's presidential race is a tight one, with President Lula da Silva up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former president, according to NPR. Nothing is settled unless a candidate takes more than half the vote. If neither does, the two meet again on Oct. 25.

sources.title: Q3’s Horror Box Office Shows the Trouble with Always Hunting Another ‘Obsession’

discussion.body: The interesting split here is between the surprises and the sure things. A big arrival for a known franchise and a hit built by a title like Buddy say different things about where the audience actually went.
Both readings can be true of the same three months, which is the point. Pick the winner and the quarter looks healthy; pick the franchise that had to weigh its own costs and the picture changes.

items.title: Q3 Horror Had One Big Opening and a Few Cost-Benefit Reckonings
items.body: IndieWire's account of horror's third quarter splits two ways. Resident Evil arrived big and Buddy built a hit, while Evil Dead and Insidious ran into cost-benefit expectations — the gap between what a film costs and what it is asked to return. The outlet's argument is that a genre's quarter cannot be read off a single title: one benchmark is not enough to say how horror actually did.

sources.title: Debris spotted from missing Ontario air ambulance

items.title: Debris From a Missing Ontario Air Ambulance Spotted Off the U.S. Coast
items.body: Global News reports debris from a missing Ontario air ambulance has been spotted off the coast of the United States. The aircraft had been carrying six people, including four Canadians.
